source_text: Εἴποιτε ἂν οὖν συνέσει πάντας ὑπερέχοντες· Τίνι οὖν τῷ λόγῳ ἔνια τῶν εἰδώλων ἐνεργεῖ, εἰ μή εἰσι θεοὶ ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἱδρυόμεθα τὰ ἀγάλματα; Οὐ γὰρ εἰκὸς τὰς ἀψύχους καὶ ἀκινήτους εἰκόνας καθ᾿ ἑαυτὰς ἰσχύειν χωρὶς τοῦ κινοῦντος. Τὸ μὲν δὴ κατὰ τόπους καὶ πόλεις καὶ ἔθνη γίνεσθαί τινας ἐπ᾿ ὀνόματι εἰδώλων ἐνεργείας οὐδ᾿ ἡμεῖς ἀντιλέγομεν· οὐ μήν, εἰ ὠφελήθησάν τινες καὶ αὖ ἐλυπήθησαν ἕτεροι, θεοὺς νομιοῦμεν τοὺς ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα ἐνεργήσαντας. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ᾧ λόγῳ νομίζετε ἰσχύειν τὰ εἴδωλα, καὶ τίνες οἱ ἐνεργοῦντες, ἐπιβατεύοντες αὐτῶν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν, ἐπ᾿ ἀκριβὲς ἐξητάκαμεν. Ἀναγκαῖον δέ μοι, μέλλοντι δεικνύειν τίνες οἱ ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰδώλοις ἐνεργοῦντες καὶ ὅτι μὴ θεοί, προσχρήσασθαί τισι καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ φιλοσοφίας μάρτυσι. Πρῶτος Θαλῆς διαιρεῖ, ὡς οἱ τὰ ἐκείνου ἀκριβοῦντες μνημονεύουσιν, εἰς θεόν, εἰς δαίμονας, εἰς ἥρωας. Ἀλλὰ θεὸν μὲν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ κόσμου ἄγει, δαίμονας δὲ οὐσίας νοεῖ ψυχικάς, καὶ ἥρωας τὰς κεχωρισμένας ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἀγαθοὺς μὲν τὰς ἀγαθάς, κακοὺς δὲ τὰς φαύλας. Πλάτων δέ, τὰ ἄλλα ἐπέχων, καὶ αὐτὸς εἴς τε τὸν ἀγένητον θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀγενήτου εἰς κόσμον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ γεγονότας, τούς τε πλάνητας καὶ τοὺς ἀπλανεῖς ἀστέρας, καὶ εἰς δαίμονας τέμνει· περὶ ὧν δαιμόνων αὐτὸς ἀπαξιῶν λέγειν τοῖς περὶ αὐτῶν εἰρηκόσιν προσέχειν ἀξιοῖ. Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων δαιμόνων εἰπεῖν καὶ γνῶναι τὴν γένεσιν μεῖζον ἢ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς, πειστέον δὲ τοῖς εἰρηκόσιν ἔμπροσθεν, ἐγγόνοις μὲν θεῶν οὖσιν ὡς ἔφασαν, σαφῶς γέ που τοὺς ἑαυτῶν προγόνους εἰδότων· ἀδύνατον οὖν θεῶν παισὶν ἀπιστεῖν, κἄνπερ ἄνευ εἰκότων καὶ ἀναγκαίων ἀποδείξεων λέγωσιν, ἀλλὰ ὡς οἰκεῖα φασκόντων ἀπαγγέλλειν ἑπομένους τῷ νόμῳ πιστευτέον. Οὕτως οὖν κατ᾿ ἐκείνους καὶ ἡμῖν ἡ γένεσις περὶ αὐτῶν τῶν θεῶν ἐχέτω καὶ λεγέσθω. Γῆς τε καὶ Οὐρανοῦ παῖδες Ὠκεανός τε καὶ Τηθὺς ἐγεννήθησαν, τούτων δὲ Φόρκος Κρόνος τε καὶ Ῥέα καὶ ὅσοι μετὰ τούτων, ἐκ δὲ Κρόνου τε καὶ Ῥέας Ζεὺς Ἥρα τε καὶ πάντες, οὓς ἴσμεν πάντας ἀδελφοὺς λεγομένους αὐτῶν, ἔτι τε τούτων ἄλλους ἐκγόνους. Ἆρ᾿ οὖν ὁ τὸν ἀΐδιον νοῦν καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον περινοήσας θεὸν καὶ τὰ ἐπισυμβεβηκότα αὐτῷ ἐξειπών, τὸ ὄντως ὄν, τὸ μονοφυές, τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἀποχεόμενον, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀλήθεια, καὶ περὶ πρώτης δυνάμεως, καὶ ὡς περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα πάντα ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκείνου ἕνεκεν πάντα, καὶ ἐκεῖνο αἴτιον πάντων, καὶ περὶ δύο καὶ τρία, δεύτερον δὲ περὶ τὰ δεύτερα, καὶ τρίτον περὶ τὰ τρίτα, περὶ τῶν ἐκ τῶν αἰσθητῶν γῆς τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ λεγομένων γεγονέναι μεῖζον ἢ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν τἀληθὲς μαθεῖν ἐνόμισεν; Ἦ οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν. Ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ ἀδύνατον γεννᾶν καὶ ἀποκυΐσκεσθαι θεοὺς ἐνόμισεν, ἑπομένων τοῖς γινομένοις τελῶν, καί, τὸ τούτου ἀδυνατώτερον, μεταπεῖσαι τοὺς πολλοὺς ἀβασανίστως τοὺς μύθους παραδεχομένους, διὰ ταῦτα μεῖζον ἢ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν γνῶναι καὶ εἰπεῖν ἔφη περὶ τῆς τῶν ἄλλων δαιμόνων γενέσεως, οὔτε μαθεῖν οὔτε ἐξειπεῖν γεννᾶσθαι θεοὺς δυνάμενος. Καὶ τὸ εἰρημένον αὐτῷ· Ὁ δὴ μέγας ἡγεμὼν ἐν οὐρανῷ Ζεύς, ἐλαύνων πτηνὸν ἅρμα, πρῶτος πορεύεται διακοσμῶν πάντα καὶ ἐπιμελούμενος, τῷ δὲ ἕπεται στρατιὰ θεῶν τε καὶ δαιμόνων· οὐκ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀπὸ Κρόνου λεγομένου ἔχει Διός. Ἔστι γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ ὄνομα τῷ ποιητῇ τῶν ὅλων. Δηλοῖ δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Πλάτων· ἑτέρῳ σημαντικῷ προσειπεῖν αὐτὸν οὐκ ἔχων τῷ δημώδει ὀνόματι, οὐχ ὡς ἰδίῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀλλ᾿ εἰς σαφήνειαν, ὅτι μὴ δυνατὸν εἰς πάντας φέρειν κατὰ δύναμιν τὸν θεόν, προσεχρήσατο, ἐπικατηγορήσας τὸ μέγας, ἵνα διαστείλῃ τὸν οὐράνιον ἀπὸ τοῦ χαμᾶθεν, τὸν ἀγένητον ἀπὸ τοῦ γενητοῦ, τοῦ νεωτέρου μὲν οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, νεωτέρου δὲ Κρητῶν, οἳ ἐξέκλεψαν αὐτὸν μὴ ἀναιρεθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός.
pass_a_gloss: You would say therefore being superior in understanding to all; By what reason then do some of the idols have power, if they are not gods on which we base the statues? For it is not likely that the lifeless and motionless images have power by themselves without the one moving them. That indeed in places and cities and nations some things come to be in the name of idol powers we do not contradict; not at all, if some were helped and others were grieved, we consider those who worked on both sides to be gods. But also by what reason you think the idols have power, and who are the ones working, going on to their names, we have examined precisely. It is necessary for me, about to show who are the ones working on the idols and that they are not gods, to use also some witnesses from philosophy. First Thales divides, as those who carefully examine his things remember, into god, into demons, into heroes. But he considers god to be the mind of the world, demons to be psychic substances, and heroes to be the separated souls of men, the good ones being good, the bad ones being bad. Plato also, holding to other things, and himself too, cuts into the ungenerated god and the ones generated by the ungenerated into the world of heaven, the planets and the fixed stars, and into demons; concerning which demons he himself considers it worthy to pay attention to those who have spoken about them. Concerning the other demons, to speak and know their generation is greater than us; one must believe those who spoke before, being offspring of gods as they said, clearly knowing their own ancestors; it is impossible therefore to disbelieve the children of gods, even if they speak without likely and necessary proofs, but as if they are speaking about their own family, following the law, they are to be believed. Thus therefore, according to them, and also to us, let the generation concerning the gods be had and spoken. Earth and Heaven were born, and Ocean and Tethys, and from them Phorcus and Cronus and Rhea and as many as after them, and from Cronus and Rhea Zeus and Hera and all whom we know, all being called their brothers, and also others born from them. Would one who has understood the eternal mind and the one comprehended by reason, and having explained the things that have happened to him, the truly existing, the single-generated, the good flowing from him, which is truth, and concerning the first power, and how all things are concerning the king of all, and all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all, and concerning two and three, the second concerning the seconds, and the third concerning the thirds, concerning the things said to have been generated from the sensible earth and heaven, consider it greater than the truth itself to learn? Or is it not possible to say. But since it is impossible to generate and give birth to gods, he considered, following the things that happen, and also, it is more impossible to persuade the many, who accept the myths without examination, on account of these things, he said that it is greater than the truth itself to know and speak concerning the generation of the other demons, being unable to generate or give birth to gods. And what was said to him: The great leader in heaven Zeus, driving a winged chariot, first goes, adorning all and taking care, and a army of gods and demons follows him; this does not apply to the Zeus said to be from Cronus. For there is in this a name of the poet of all things. Plato also shows; not having another significant word to add to the popular name, not as if it were the private name of god, but for clarity, that it is not possible to bear the god according to power to all, he used, adding the great, so that he might distinguish the heavenly from the earthly, the ungenerated from the generated, of the newer heaven and earth, newer also than the Cretans, who stole him so that he would not be destroyed by his father.
pass_b_english: You might claim to surpass everyone in understanding, yet by what reason do some idols exercise power if they are not the gods on whom we base our statues? It is not plausible that lifeless, motionless images possess power of themselves apart from the one who moves them. We do not deny that certain effects occur in various places, cities, and nations under the name of idol-powers; but even if some people were helped and others harmed, we do not therefore regard those who worked on both sides as gods. Moreover, we have precisely investigated by what reason you believe the idols have power and who the agents are who ride upon their names. Since I am about to demonstrate who operates through the idols and that they are not gods, I must also call on witnesses from philosophy. First, Thales divides reality into God, demons, and heroes, as those who carefully study his teachings recall. He identifies God as the mind of the world, demons as psychic substances, and heroes as the separated souls of human beings—good souls counted as good, bad souls as bad. Plato, while maintaining his other doctrines, likewise cuts reality into the ungenerated God and those generated by the ungenerated into the world of heaven—the planets and the fixed stars—and into demons. Concerning these demons he himself deems it unworthy to speak, urging attention to those who have spoken about them. As for the other demons, to speak and know their generation is beyond us; we must believe those who spoke before, since they are offspring of gods, as they said, and clearly know their own ancestors. It is therefore impossible to disbelieve the children of gods, even if they speak without likely and necessary proofs, but as those claiming to report their own family matters; following the law, they are to be believed. Thus, according to them and also to us, let the genealogy concerning these gods be accepted and stated. Earth and Heaven were born, and Ocean and Tethys; from them came Phorcus, Cronus, and Rhea, and as many as followed them; from Cronus and Rhea came Zeus and Hera and all whom we know, all called their brothers, and still others born from them. Would one who has grasped the eternal mind and comprehended it by reason, and has explained the attributes belonging to it—the truly existent, the single-generated, the good flowing from it, which is truth, and concerning the first power, and how all things relate to the king of all, and all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all, and concerning two and three, the second concerning the seconds, and the third concerning the thirds—consider it a greater task than truth itself to learn the truth concerning the things said to have been generated from the sensible earth and heaven? That cannot be said. But since he regarded it as impossible for gods to be begotten and born, following the consequences of that view, and, what is even more impossible, to persuade the multitude to accept myths without examination, he declared that to know and speak concerning the generation of the other demons is greater than truth itself, since he was unable to learn or declare that gods are begotten. And what was said to him: 'The great leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them, and a host of gods and demons follows him'—this does not apply to the Zeus said to be from Cronus. For in this passage the name belongs to the poet of all things. Plato himself indicates this: lacking another significant term to add to the common name, not as if it were the god's own private name but for clarity, because it is not possible to convey the god according to his power to everyone, he employed the epithet 'great' in order to distinguish the heavenly from the earthly, the ungenerated from the generated—of the newer heaven and earth, newer also than the Cretans, who stole him away so that he would not be killed by his father.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex philosophical distinctions of Athenagoras regarding Thales and Plato. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek text. Pass B provides a more fluent rendering of the conditional and relative clauses without altering the theological or philosophical meaning. All clauses, including the specific divisions of Thales and the Platonic distinctions between the ungenerated and generated, are preserved.
The translation accurately reflects the Greek text, with proper handling of names, terms, and citations. No errors in source identity, completeness, or doctrinal accuracy were found.
